2. The facts, in short, are that the present appellant as pre-emptor filed miscellaneous case for pre-emption under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, as a co-sharer of the disputed land, while the pre-emptee-purchasers (opposite party Nos. 1 and 2) are strangers. The land was sold by another co-sharer pre-emptee-seller (opposite party No. 3) to the purchasers via a registered kabala dated 09.05.2010 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor. Upon knowing about the sale, the pre-emptor filed the said miscellaneous case for pre-emption within the statutory period, depositing the requisite amount, asserting her entitlement to get pre-emption of the land. 

 6. He also argues that the cause of action of this case for pre-emption started on the very date of execution and registration of the kabala in question and also on the date when the pre-emptor got knowledge of the said sale deed and both these facts have been elaborately stated both in the application for pre-emption and also in deposition before the trial court, but inspite of that both the trial Court and the High Court Division most illegally held that the cause of action of this case has not been proved. 

 10. The intention of the legislature, as out-lined in Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, is clear to prevent any outsiders from encroaching upon the ownership and possession of the rightful co-sharers. This ensures that the legitimate co-sharers can continue to enjoy their property without interference from others. The right of pre-emption on the basis of the petitioner being a co-sharer of the tenancy must be proved to the hilt. One cannot succeed on establishing a prima facie case. When the dispute has to be finally adjudicated, the proof of the claim must be established by cogent and reliable evidence.
